card.description: Data-driven ranking of neighborhoods. Won "Best GUI" at CONVENE 2k24.

title: NESS — Neighborhood Evaluation & Scoring System.
page.subtitle: A data-driven ranking engine for neighborhoods. Pulls from Google Maps, layers analytics on top, and surfaces a livability score you can actually trust. Awarded "Best GUI" at CONVENE 2k24.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: City life is full of invisible trade-offs — safety here, air quality there, schools over there. NESS flattens all of that into something you can read at a glance: a ranked score per neighborhood, backed by data.

We pulled civic and location data, ran it through a Flask analytics backend, and rendered the results in a React interface that judges called the cleanest in the room. The "Best GUI" trophy at CONVENE 2k24 wasn't a fluke — it was the whole point.

sections.heading: What I built
list: React frontend with interactive Maps overlay and live-updating scores
Flask analytics service combining multiple data signals into one rank
A comparison view so users could weigh two neighborhoods head-to-head
End-to-end design — from judge-pleasing UI to the color system used throughout

sections.heading: Stack
sections.stackLine: React · Google Maps API · Flask · Python · Pandas · Plotly

card.description: AI-optimized daily schedules, plugged into Google Calendar.

title: Smart Scheduler.
Your calendar, thought about.
page.subtitle: A planner that looks at your todos, your prescheduled events and what time of day you actually get things done — then proposes a schedule you'd have written yourself, if you had the time.

meta.stack: React · Gemini API· Google Calendar API

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Most scheduling tools treat time as a container — here's a slot, shove a task in. Smart Scheduler treats time like the scarce, opinionated resource it actually is: you don't do deep work at 9pm, you don't take meetings before coffee, and Tuesdays feel different than Thursdays.
Feed it a list of todos plus your existing calendar, and it proposes a day that makes sense. Approve with one click and it writes back to Google Calendar.

sections.heading: Details
list: Gemini plans the day using task metadata + time-of-day preferences
Reads/writes Google Calendar via OAuth
Drag-to-refine — you can override the AI without starting over
React frontend with keyboard-first interaction

card.description: Elliptic-curve signed messaging on Firebase real-time DB.

title: Chat-LECS.
Messages that sign themselves.
page.subtitle: A chat app where every message carries a Linear Elliptic Curve Signature — so recipients can mathematically verify the sender, not just trust a username. Firebase underneath, real-time everywhere.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Chat apps ask you to trust the server. Chat-LECS asks you to trust the math. Every outbound message is signed with the sender's private key using elliptic-curve cryptography; every received message is verified client-side before it's rendered.
Firebase handles the real-time transport and auth. The signing layer is the interesting bit — it's what turns "probably from you" into "provably from you."

sections.heading: Details
list: ECC key pairs generated and stored client-side at registration
Each message signed before upload, verified on download
Firebase real-time DB for transport, Firebase Auth for identity
Visual indicator per-message for verification state
Multi device support

card.description: Benchmarks sorting algorithms across single and multi-threaded runs. Built in C++ with OpenMP.

title: Sort-Alyzer.
Big-O is a lie until you measure.
page.subtitle: A C++ tool that runs every classic sorting algorithm against the same inputs — single-threaded, and multi-threaded with OpenMP. The results never match the textbook. That's the whole point.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Textbook complexity hides a lot — cache misses, branch prediction, memory allocator warmup, the fact that your laptop throttles when it gets warm. Sort-Alyzer just runs the sorts and measures what actually happens.

I wrote clean implementations of quick, merge, heap, radix, bubble, insertion and shell sort, then wrapped them in an OpenMP harness that can parallelize the divide-step where it makes sense. The output is a little less like a CS exam and more like truth.

sections.heading: Details
list: 7 sorting algorithms, hand-written in modern C++
OpenMP parallelization for divide-and-conquer sorts
Micro-benchmark harness with warmup + statistical runs
Exports to CSV for offline plotting

card.description: Rips a Spotify playlist to MP3 via YouTube. Reserach Purpose only. Does not endorse copyright infringement.

title: SoundScrapper.
Playlist in, MP3s out.
page.subtitle: Point it at a Spotify playlist. It reads the tracklist, finds each song on YouTube, and hands you a folder of MP3s. Built for the times streaming won't do. Built for only educational purpose and does not motivates unautorized access to copyrighted music.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Built this for long flights, bad data, and the particular joy of owning an MP3. Drop in a playlist URL; Spotify's API gives us the tracklist; YouTube handles matching and audio; YTDL-Core pulls the audio down; it lands as tagged MP3s in a folder. Doesn't endorse copyright infringement.

sections.heading: Details
list: Spotify API for playlist + track metadata
YouTube search for best-match source video
YTDL-Core to extract audio streams
Progress UI written in React, queues + retries

card.description: A space shooter built in C++ with SFML. Expanding window mechanic, custom art.

title: ShootIt++.
A space shooter that grows on you.
page.subtitle: Old-school arcade shooter written in C++ with SFML. Custom graphics, custom sound, and a mechanic that nobody asked for: shoot enough asteroids and the game window literally expands.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Wrote this the year I discovered C++ graphics could be fun. SFML handles the window, input, and sprite rendering; I wrote the physics, the collision, the sound cues, the asteroid spawner and the UI.

The expanding-window thing was a whim that became the best part of the game. Hit enough asteroids and the playable area literally grows — which means new asteroids spawn in new places, which means the game gets harder in a way you can see.

sections.heading: Details
list: Custom sprite art made frame-by-frame
Physics + collision in plain C++ — no engine
Progressive difficulty via the window-growth mechanic
Ambient sound and projectile SFX mixed in
